horizon_driver: Quarterly AUM/flow reporting and fee-compression competition set the commercial clock; the political clock (state-AG lawsuits, SEC/DOJ leadership, election-driven anti-ESG or pro-ESG swings) resets on a 2-4 year cycle and has recently dominated the commercial one. Treat as short-horizon (~1yr effective) because legal/political exposure is what has actually moved behavior since 2023, not multi-year investment theses.

capabilities.note: Maintain current index-tracking weights and default (delegated or house) proxy-voting policy. The modal action on ~99% of AUM at any time; deviation from benchmark is itself a fireable offense for a fund manager here.

Comply with an external rule change without resistance: rebalance to a new index composition, vote with management, exit or re-enter a coalition/label (NZAM, Climate Action 100+) when legal/political exposure changes, launch a pass-through/proxy-choice voting option to defuse pressure. This is the dominant response to state-AG or federal pressure observed 2024-2025.

Contested proxy vote against management/board, public break with a client-state's mandate (e.g., refusing a state treasurer's divestment order and litigating it), or an index-provider decision to exclude/include a security for political rather than liquidity/free-float reasons (e.g., the 2022 Russia deletion). Rare, high-salience, and irreversible in effect even though the underlying holding can technically be rebought.

constraints.source: fiduciary duty / ERISA and prospectus tracking-error mandates for index products
constraints.breaks_under: effectively never for true index funds; this is the one constraint in the dossier that is closer to physics than to policy

constraints.source: 2018-2023 stakeholder-capitalism branding (Larry Fink's annual CEO letters; founding membership in Net Zero Asset Managers initiative, Dec 2020)
constraints.breaks_under: state-level legal exposure crosses a low threshold — BlackRock quit NZAM within ~2 months of the Texas-led multistate antitrust suit (filed Nov 2024) naming that exact membership as evidence; Vanguard had already quit NZAM in Dec 2022 under similar pressure. Treat as a constraint that is dropped, not honored, once it becomes legally costly.

constraints.source: stewardship guidelines framed as principled ('long-term value creation')
constraints.breaks_under: any period of elevated political scrutiny from either flank — support for E&S proposals collapsed from >40% (2021 proxy season) to ~21% (2022), ~7% (2023), ~4% (2024), and under 2% (2025) at BlackRock; Vanguard supported 0% of E&S proposals in the 2024 season. The break is monotonic and pre-dates any single lawsuit, meaning it tracks the broader political mood, not one legal event.

stated_vs_revealed.stated: 2018-2022: Larry Fink's annual CEO letters framed BlackRock's scale as a vehicle for 'stakeholder capitalism' and long-horizon climate stewardship; BlackRock was a founding signatory of the Net Zero Asset Managers initiative (Dec 2020) and voted for over 40% of environmental/social shareholder proposals in the 2021 proxy season.
stated_vs_revealed.revealed: By the 2024-2025 proxy seasons, support for environmental/social shareholder proposals had fallen to ~4% and then under 2%; BlackRock formally exited NZAM on Jan 9, 2025, stating membership 'caused confusion... and subjected us to legal inquiries from various public officials' — an explicit admission the reversal was driven by state-AG legal exposure (Texas et al.'s Nov 2024 antitrust suit alleging coal-market collusion via climate coalitions), not by updated climate analysis. Vanguard quit the same initiative over two years earlier (Dec 2022) and supported 0% of E&S proposals in 2024.
stated_vs_revealed.delta: A ~40-point swing in voting behavior and a full public exit from a marquee climate commitment within about four years, admitted by the actor itself to be a response to legal/political liability rather than a change in view. This is the single largest and best-documented stated-vs-revealed gap for this actor: 'stewardship principles' function as a liability-management dial, not a fixed value.

stated_vs_revealed.stated: Index providers (MSCI, FTSE Russell) present index construction and inclusion/exclusion as a rules-based, apolitical, liquidity- and free-float-driven methodology, and asset managers present their consequent buying/selling as mechanical rebalancing.
stated_vs_revealed.revealed: In March 2022, MSCI and FTSE Russell deleted all Russian equities from their emerging-market indices at a price of zero, a decision driven by sanctions and capital controls rather than any liquidity formula in the published methodology, forcing every benchmarked fund (passive and closet-index active alike) to write the position to zero simultaneously, with no ability to sell first. This is the clearest empirical proof that 'index inclusion' is a geopolitically triggerable chokepoint, not a neutral clerical process, and that AM_INDEX's mandate rigidity (it must follow the rule regardless of price or timing) is exactly what the Cartographer flagged.
stated_vs_revealed.delta: Methodology is described as apolitical and mechanical; in the one clean natural experiment available (Russia 2022), a geopolitical/sanctions event, not a liquidity metric, drove the deletion, and every rule-following fund was forced to transact (or rather, forced to accept a zero mark with no transaction possible) in lockstep.

dependencies.note: AM_INDEX does not itself decide index composition for most benchmarks (MSCI/FTSE/S&P are legally distinct index providers), but is contractually bound to follow their calls near-instantly. This is the actor's single largest external dependency and the main channel through which a geopolitical event becomes a forced flow.

State attorneys general (Texas-led coalition) and federal regulators (SEC rulemaking on proxy voting, ERISA fiduciary guidance) set the boundaries of what stewardship activity is legally safe; this has been the dominant driver of behavior change since 2023.

tripwires.if: a state attorney general or multistate coalition files or threatens litigation naming a specific climate/ESG coalition membership as evidence of anti-competitive conduct
tripwires.then: AM_INDEX exits that coalition within one quarter regardless of prior public commitment, and issues a statement that the exit 'won't change how we manage investments' — observed pattern: BlackRock exited NZAM ~2 months after the Nov 2024 Texas suit; the entire NZAM initiative suspended operations days later (Jan 13, 2025) once the largest members had left.

tripwires.if: MSCI/FTSE/S&P announce a reclassification or deletion of a market or security (sanctions, capital-control, or liquidity-driven)
tripwires.then: AM_INDEX's passive vehicles execute the resulting reallocation within the index provider's effective date (typically days to a few weeks), regardless of price, realized-loss recognition, or client preference — this is close to a hard rule, not a judgment call.

tripwires.if: a red state (e.g., Texas, Florida, Oklahoma) or blue state pulls or threatens to pull public pension mandates over the manager's ESG posture in either direction
tripwires.then: the manager adjusts public messaging and, where possible, offers segregated/choice voting products (BlackRock's, Vanguard's, and State Street's 2023-2025 rollout of pass-through and voting-choice programs for index funds) rather than take a public political side — the actor optimizes for AUM retention across the political spectrum, not for a consistent ideological position.

what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that BlackRock, Vanguard, or State Street sustained a costly stewardship position (support for shareholder proposals, coalition membership, or a specific vote against management) *after* it became legally or politically costly to a specific state government, rather than folding within one to two quarters, would meaningfully raise the credibility score on stewardship commitments. Conversely, an actual antitrust breakup or forced-divestiture ruling (rather than settled/dismissed litigation) would lower the survival_threshold materially, since it would be the first real test of the 'too big to break up' assumption embedded in the low survival weight.
